overview: Eric IX of Sweden was Swedish king remembered as Saint Erik, a royal saint whose historical life is less clear than his later cult. The profile is anchored by concrete turning points: c. 1156 — Rules as king; traditionally 1150s — Mission or crusade traditions; 1160 — Killed.
He died in 1160, and his reign belongs to the wider story of Scandinavian state formation, Christianization, dynastic conflict, and northern Europe’s ties to England, the Baltic, and the Empire.

contentSections.title: Overview

contentSections.title: Birth and early life
paragraphs: Eric IX of Sweden was born c. 1125. His family background is usually placed in House of Erik, though early Scandinavian genealogy can be uncertain and politically shaped.
Eric IX of Sweden's early life belonged to the medieval Scandinavian world, where kinship, sea routes, church contacts, assemblies, and armed followings shaped the opportunities available to a ruler.

contentSections.title: Character and Personality
paragraphs: Eric IX of Sweden became Sweden's patron saint, and his remembered character, like Olaf of Norway's, is shaped decisively by that cult. The hagiographic tradition presents him as a model Christian king — just, pious, protective of the church, and a crusader who carried Christianity to the Finns — and credits him with a martyr's death, killed by political enemies, by tradition after hearing mass, around 1160.

This portrait comes almost entirely from the legend composed to support his sainthood, written well after his death, so its specific virtues must be read as the qualities a holy king was expected to display rather than as documented biography. The historical Eric is correspondingly hard to recover beneath the saint.

What the tradition consistently conveys is the image of the righteous royal martyr: devout, law-giving, and zealous in the faith. Whether the man matched the legend cannot be established, but the cult fixed his reputation firmly as Sweden's holy king, and that devotional memory is most of what survives of his character.

contentSections.title: As king and saint
paragraphs: Eric IX ruled in the mid-twelfth century and became a major saintly figure in Swedish royal and civic memory. Later traditions link him to crusading in Finland, though the evidence is debated.
As King of Sweden, Saint, Eric IX of Sweden had to turn dynastic claim into workable authority through alliances, military pressure, church support, and acceptance by regional elites.

contentSections.title: Death
paragraphs: Killed in 1160, traditionally at Uppsala after Mass; his cult later became central to Swedish royal sanctity.

contentSections.title: Legacy
paragraphs: His legacy is as important for sanctity and national memory as for reconstructable politics.
Later saga, saintly, or national traditions often amplified Eric IX of Sweden's reputation, so the article separates near-contemporary evidence from later memory where possible.

timeline.title: Born
timeline.description: Eric IX of Sweden was born around c. 1125, but the birthplace is not securely recorded. The date is approximate, but it places the early life in the setting of Kingdom of Sweden.

timeline.title: Rules as king
timeline.description: Eric IX ruled in mid-twelfth-century Sweden and later became the focus of a royal saintly cult.

timeline.title: Mission or crusade traditions
timeline.description: Later tradition connected Eric with a Finnish crusade and missionary activity, but the historical details are difficult to verify.

timeline.title: Killed
timeline.description: Killed in 1160, traditionally at Uppsala after Mass; his cult later became central to Swedish royal sanctity.

timeline.title: Aftermath and memory
timeline.description: Eric’s posthumous cult made him a royal saint and symbol of Swedish kingship, even where the details of his reign and alleged crusade remain uncertain.

predecessor.note: Murdered on his way to church in 1156

successor.note: Magnus Henriksson killed St Eric in 1160 and usurped the throne; he was in turn overthrown and killed by Charles VII Sverkersson in 1161.
